title: French Bulldog
wiki_lead: The French Bulldog (French: Bouledogue Français) also known as the Frenchie, is a French breed of companion dog or toy dog. It appeared in Paris in the mid-nineteenth century, apparently the result of cross-breeding of Toy Bulldogs imported from England and local Parisian ratters. It is commonly kept as a pet and is among the most frequently registered dogs in a number of countries including Australia, the United Kingdom, and the United States. The breed is susceptible to various health problems due to being bred for its distinctive flat face and skin wrinkles.
wiki_excerpt:
The French Bulldog (French: Bouledogue Français) also known as the Frenchie, is a French breed of companion dog or toy dog. It appeared in Paris in the mid-nineteenth century, apparently the result of cross-breeding of Toy Bulldogs imported from England and local Parisian ratters. It is commonly kept as a pet and is among the most frequently registered dogs in a number of countries including Australia, the United Kingdom, and the United States. The breed is susceptible to various health problems due to being bred for its distinctive flat face and skin wrinkles.


History
From the beginning of the nineteenth century, bulldogs were bred in the United Kingdom for purposes other than traditional blood sports such as bull-baiting, which were banned in 1835. By the middle of the century there were miniature bulldogs, most weighing around 7–11 kg (15–24 lb).
At the same time, lace workers from Nottingham who were displaced by the Industrial Revolution began to settle in Normandy, France. They brought a variety of dogs with them, including Toy Bulldogs. The dogs became popular in France and a trade in imported small Bulldogs was created, with breeders in England sending over Bulldogs that they considered to be too small, or with faults such as ears that stood up. By 1860, there were few Toy Bulldogs left in England, such was their popularity in France.
The small Bulldog type gradually became thought of as a breed, and received a name, the Bouledogue Français. This French version of the English name is also a contraction of the words boule ('ball') and dogue ('mastiff'). The dogs were highly fashionable and were sought after by society ladies and Parisian prostitutes alike, as well as creators such as artists, writers, and fashion designers. The artists Edgar Degas and Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec are thought to have French Bulldogs in their paintings. However, records were not kept of the breed's development as it diverged further away from its original Bulldog roots. As it changed, terrier stock had been brought in to develop traits such as the breed's long straight ears.

Breed clubs and modern recognition
Americans had been importing French Bulldogs for a while, but it was not until 1885 that they were brought over in order to set up an American-based breeding program. They were mostly owned by society ladies, who first displayed them at the Westminster Kennel Club Dog Show in 1896. In the following year, the judge at the dog show, George Raper, only chose winners with "rose ears"—ears that folded at the tip, as with the standard for Bulldogs. grok_lead: The French Bulldog is a small, muscular companion dog breed renowned for its distinctive bat-like ears, square head with wrinkles, and compact, heavy-boned build that resembles a miniature Bulldog. Affectionate, playful, and adaptable, it thrives in urban environments and forms strong bonds with families, children, and other pets while serving as an alert but minimally vocal watchdog. Typically standing 11 to 13 inches tall at the shoulder and weighing no more than 28 pounds, the breed has a smooth, short coat in colors like fawn, brindle, or white, and an average lifespan of 10 to 12 years. The breed's origins trace back to 19th-century England, where smaller "toy" versions of the English Bulldog were developed after the 1835 ban on bull-baiting, particularly among Nottingham's lace-making community who favored compact dogs for ratting and companionship. Displaced by industrialization, these English workers migrated to northern France in the 1850s and 1860s, bringing their dogs, which interbred with local terriers and were refined in Paris to emphasize erect "bat" ears over the rose ears of traditional Bulldogs. Gaining popularity across French social strataâfrom working-class butchers and artists to the aristocracy during the Belle Ãpoque âthe French Bulldog arrived in the United States in the late 19th century via tourists and expatriates, leading to the formation of the first breed club in 1897 and American Kennel Club recognition in 1898. In terms of temperament, French Bulldogs are even-tempered, intelligent, and eager to please, though they can exhibit stubbornness that benefits from early socialization and positive reinforcement training. Their gait is free and vigorous with a four-track pattern, supported by short, stout forelegs and muscular hindquarters, while their roach back and tucked abdomen contribute to a balanced, pear-shaped silhouette. Care involves weekly brushing to maintain the glossy coat, regular cleaning of facial folds to prevent infections, and moderate daily exercise like short walks, as they overheat easily and cannot swim due to their structure. Health-wise, French Bulldogs are prone to brachycephalic obstructive airway syndrome (BOAS), which causes breathing difficulties exacerbated by their short muzzle, as well as eye issues like cherry eye or entropion, skin allergies, and intervertebral disc disease. They also face risks from obesity, heat sensitivity, and anesthesia complications, necessitating veterinary screening for breeding and a diet to control weight. Despite these concerns, the breed's charm has propelled it to the top of American Kennel Club registrations, ranking as the most popular dog breed in the United States for the third consecutive year in 2024.
